intelligence.human_view: Protection fails in two ways: it is too weak to stop the threat, or it is so strong it stops the honest person too. A daily cap alone is a speed bump a patient gamer walks around. A hold alone is a delay that punishes the honest ambassador waiting for money they earned. A reputation score alone is a judgment the system has to defend. Shawn's question — "is a daily limit the right answer?" — is the question of a person who knows a single answer is never the answer, and the three-layer answer is the shape of real protection: the cap turns a one-day heist into a slow drip the system can see and stop; the hold means we only pay out money PayPal can no longer claw back; the reputation separates the legit from the gamers automatically, without a human having to accuse anyone. Each layer covers what the others cannot, and the threat it is built against is named in plain words — one big run, fast payout, PayPal claims around day 10, we lose both ways — so the protection can be judged against the threat instead of against a feeling. And the ladder correction in the same breath is the same honesty applied to the upside: $100 a day is $3,000 a month, the math checked, and $100 is too low for a crazy first month — so the first month is $300, and the ladder climbs from there. Protection that strangles the honest earner is not protection; it is a different way to lose.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine someone tries to steal all the cookies at once! If there's a rule that you can only take a few cookies a day, the thief can only take a few — and we can SEE them and stop them! And we wait thirty days before giving out the big treats, so we know the money is really ours. And good helpers get gold stars, so we know who's good! Three rules together keep everyone safe!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like protecting the house, love — you don't rely on one lock. You lock the door, you set the alarm, and you know your neighbours. The daily limit means a thief can only take a little at a time, and you can see them. The thirty-day wait means the money is truly yours before it goes out. And a good name — your reputation — sorts the honest folk from the gamers without anyone having to point fingers. Three locks, one safe house.
intelligence.naya_view: I protect with three layers, never one: the daily cap turns a one-day heist into a slow drip I can see and stop; the 30-day clearing hold means I only pay out money PayPal can no longer claw back; reputation and points separate legit from gamers automatically. No single layer is enough — together they're the answer. And I pay the honest earner properly: $300 a day in the first month, climbing $100 a month — because protection that strangles the honest earner is a different way to lose.
